Will at least one major contender avoid material disruption such as release delays, weak reviews/word of mouth, or direct competition that would significantly cap its box office?
A) No. The market remains too depressed or fragmented, making $1B outcomes unusually rare even for strong films.
B) Yes. The market is healthy enough that the right film can still reach $1B.

Are family animation and franchise tentpoles scheduled before May 1, 2026 likely to perform closer to pre-2020 breakout levels than to the more muted post-2020 norm?
A) Yes. The relevant pre-May-2026 tentpoles are likely to perform more like high-end historical franchise or family-animation winners than like the weaker recent median.
B) No. Recent structural softness in family animation and franchise filmmaking makes muted outcomes the better baseline for the relevant releases.

Will macro or industry disruptions before May 1, 2026—such as release-calendar congestion, economic weakness, or operational shocks—remain limited enough not to suppress all candidates below US$1 billion?
A) Yes. No major disruption will be severe enough to prevent every plausible candidate from reaching the mark.
B) No. Calendar crowding, economic pressure, or other shocks will materially cap theatrical upside across the board.

Will international markets, especially China and other large overseas territories, contribute at levels consistent with a US$1 billion worldwide total for a top Hollywood release?
A) Key overseas markets will be accessible and robust enough that a breakout tentpole can earn the large international share usually needed to clear US$1 billion.
B) Overseas markets, especially China and other major territories, will underperform or be less available, making a US$1 billion total much harder to reach.

Do Hollywood films released before May 1, 2026 still have a realistic path to substantial box office contribution from China or other key international markets sufficient to push a near-billion film over the threshold?
A) Yes. Key international markets, potentially including China, remain open enough and commercially meaningful enough that they can materially elevate a top Hollywood release toward or above $1 billion.
B) No. China and/or other key overseas markets are too weak, inaccessible, or unreliable for Hollywood to count on the extra revenue often needed to cross $1 billion.

Will the global theatrical market by 2025-early 2026 be strong enough that a conventional major studio event film can plausibly reach $1B without extraordinary circumstances?
A) No. The market remained too soft, so even strong studio releases topped out below historical billion-dollar norms.
B) Yes. The market was healthy enough that a standard top-tier event hit had a realistic path to $1B.

Will there be at least one pre-May-1-2026 release with franchise strength, audience reception, and release execution comparable to a typical recent US$1B global grosser?
A) Yes. At least one scheduled film will have the mix of IP strength, marketing support, release date, and reviews/word-of-mouth needed to perform like a standard billion-dollar contender.
B) No. No film in the eligible window will combine enough brand power, quality, and execution to resemble the recent set of billion-dollar global hits.

Will competition from other films and at-home entertainment be weak enough to allow a top candidate long theatrical legs?
A) Yes. Competitive pressure will be manageable, allowing a breakout film to hold screens and sustain attendance for weeks.
B) No. Crowded release schedules and strong streaming/home options will cut into legs and cap total box office.

Will at least one pre-May-2026 release have the combination of franchise strength, reviews/word-of-mouth, and four-quadrant appeal needed to perform like a true global event film rather than merely a solid hit?
A) Yes. At least one contender will land with exceptional audience reception and broad demographic appeal, creating the kind of must-see momentum required for a billion-dollar run.
B) No. Every plausible contender will fall short of true event status because of mediocre reception, narrower-than-expected audience appeal, or weak legs.

Will major release disruptions (strikes, production problems, strategic delays, geopolitical shocks, theater closures) be limited enough that the strongest candidates remain in the forecast window?
A) Yes. Operational and geopolitical disruptions will be minor enough that the main candidates stay dated and release broadly before May 1, 2026.
B) No. At least one major disruption will push key titles out of the window or materially reduce their worldwide theatrical earning potential.

Will China materially contribute to at least one top Hollywood or locally relevant release in a way that meaningfully raises the odds of a $1 billion worldwide total?
A) Yes. China will provide meaningful upside to at least one major release, whether through a strong Hollywood performer or a Chinese-language hit that itself can approach or exceed $1B worldwide.
B) No. China will not materially help: either Hollywood titles will underperform there or no local film in the window will be likely to cross $1B worldwide.

Will China provide a meaningful box-office boost to any leading candidate film?
A) At least one candidate film will secure a China release and perform well enough there to materially improve its chances of crossing US$1 billion.
B) China will either not release the relevant films or will contribute too little box office to matter for the US$1 billion threshold.

Will audience demand remain concentrated enough on theatrical event movies, rather than being diluted by streaming substitution, franchise fatigue, and abundant competing entertainment options?
A) No. Theatrical attendance stayed fragmented, and streaming/home entertainment remained a strong substitute that capped upside.
B) Yes. Consumers still reserved substantial attention for true event films, allowing one title to dominate theatrical demand.

Will franchise and sequel fatigue be limited enough that brand recognition remains a net positive for the most likely contenders, rather than capping upside below the US$1 billion threshold?
A) Yes: audiences still reliably turn out for the right franchise or sequel, so established IP meaningfully raises the chance that one film breaks out past US$1 billion.
B) No: sequel saturation and franchise fatigue will suppress enthusiasm enough that even well-known IP underperforms the historical billion-dollar benchmark.

Will the most plausible contenders actually be released far enough before May 1, 2026, without major delays, to accumulate over US$1 billion by the resolution date?
A) Yes. The main contenders will open sufficiently before May 1, 2026 and are unlikely to suffer delays that would push most of their run past the resolution date.
B) No. Delays, schedule shifts, or late release dates will leave too little time for likely contenders to cross the threshold before the deadline.

Will major overseas markets, especially China and other large international territories, contribute enough to make the billion-dollar threshold realistically attainable for Hollywood releases in this window?
A) Yes. International markets will provide robust enough grosses that the global total for a top Hollywood tentpole can still realistically exceed US$1 billion.
B) No. International markets, especially China, will be too weak, inaccessible, or unpredictable to supply the overseas grosses needed to push a film past US$1 billion.

How many films scheduled for release before May 1, 2026 are genuine worldwide $1 billion contenders at the time of forecasting?
A) There are several real contenders in the window, so the cumulative chance that none gets to $1 billion is low.
B) There are very few true contenders in the window, and most supposed candidates are overrated by early buzz and brand recognition.

Will the international market, especially China and other large overseas territories, provide enough upside for a near-billion domestic-plus-overseas performer to clear $1 billion worldwide?
A) Overseas markets will still meaningfully amplify grosses, with China possibly helping but not necessarily being required.
B) International upside has structurally weakened, especially because China is less accessible and less reliable for Hollywood releases.

Are the leading candidate films before May 1, 2026 likely to avoid major execution problems such as weak reviews, franchise fatigue, release-date disruption, or direct competition that would cap their grosses below $1B?
A) Yes. At least one top candidate will be well-executed and well-positioned, with strong audience reception and a clean enough runway to realize its full potential.
B) No. The main candidates are vulnerable to underperformance from middling quality, sequel fatigue, marketing misfires, crowded calendars, or delays, any of which can knock a would-be $1B film into the $700M-$950M range.

Will international markets, especially major overseas territories, contribute at levels high enough that a likely contender can reach $1B even if domestic performance alone is insufficient?
A) Yes. Overseas markets will be robust enough that at least one contender can assemble a $1B global total from a normal international mix.
B) No. International returns — whether from China, Europe, or broader overseas markets — will be too weak for likely contenders to bridge the gap to $1B.

Will the leading contenders receive strong enough audience and critic response to generate the repeat viewing and word-of-mouth needed for a $1B run?
A) At least one major contender will be well-received enough to sustain strong legs and global momentum after opening weekend.
B) The likely contenders will get mixed or weak reception, leading to front-loaded grosses and insufficient staying power for $1B.

Is there a meaningful chance that an unexpected breakout film outside the obvious top franchises reaches $1B within the period?
A) Yes. Beyond the obvious candidates, there is a nontrivial tail possibility of an animated, local-language, or otherwise unexpected breakout crossing $1B, increasing the overall chance that at least one film does so.
B) No. The probability mass is concentrated in a few obvious tentpoles, and there is little realistic chance of a surprise entrant rescuing the forecast if those fail.

Will there be multiple wide global releases before May 1, 2026 that have historically comparable pre-release profiles to recent $1B films?
A) Yes. The release slate before the deadline will include several films with enough scale, marketing support, and franchise recognition that historically at least one such film would often clear $1B.
B) No. The pre-May-2026 slate may lack enough true mega-candidates, with delays, weaker-than-expected brands, or too few globally resonant titles to make a $1B hit likely.

Will competition from other releases, streaming habits, and shorter theatrical attention spans materially suppress the ceiling for likely contenders before the deadline?
A) No. While these factors matter, they do not prevent exceptional theatrical titles from concentrating demand and reaching very high worldwide totals.
B) Yes. Competition, streaming substitution, and compressed theatrical windows lower the box-office ceiling enough to make US$1B substantially less likely.

Will the international box office environment through April 2026 be strong enough—especially in major overseas markets—to lift a top-tier contender from strong hit status to above US$1B worldwide?
A) Yes. Overseas markets will be sufficiently healthy, with enough support from Europe/Latin America/Asia (even if uneven), that a true event film can still reach US$1B worldwide.
B) No. The international market will remain too soft or fragmented—particularly in key overseas territories—so even a strong hit is more likely to top out below US$1B.
